A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MCDPO research work. All 14 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original SD1.5 and SDXL experiments, component ablations, specialist comparisons, implicit reward accuracy, and training-data correlation analysis.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds conflict-only training comparisons, robustness studies, guidance analyses, and a human evaluation on 100 PickV2 prompts.

M1.justification: The stated symmetric loss changes from one negative log-sigmoid applied to the sum of both orientation margins in v1 Eq. 13 to separate negative log-sigmoids in v2 Eq. 17; these are not equivalent objectives. v2 also adds temporal aesthetic conditioning and separately weighted prompt/reward guidance in Appendix E, Eq. 24. These substantially revise the stated optimization and inference procedures, although implementation changes or reruns are not established.

E1.justification: Pick-a-Pic v2, PartiPrompts, HPDv2, and the text-to-image domain are retained. Appendix E adds corrupted-preference-label scenarios with 10% and 20% random flips, extending the training-input conditions examined. The human evaluation reuses PickV2 rather than adding a new dataset.

E2.justification: The expanded comparisons add merged conditional-DPO specialists, conflict-trained DPO, and an explicitly unfrozen full-MCSFT control in Tables 3 and 5. These materially expand controls for supervision, parameters, and conflict handling. Main benchmark comparators remain unchanged; standard DPO specialists and their merged baseline already appeared in v1 Appendix B.

E3.justification: v2 expands the existing 18%-budget comparison with conflict-only training and adds human ranking on 100 randomly sampled prompts, including mean-rank and Top-1 metrics. New sensitivity experiments vary dropout, discretization, label corruption, and guidance. Appendix C also changes the reported SD1.5 MCSFT learning rate from 1e-8 to 1e-9 and model-based reward dropout from 0.1 to 0.2; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds conflict-specific implicit-reward trajectories, generated-output agreement heatmaps, cumulative-axis and temporal-guidance analyses, and sensitivity tests for CLIP dropout, bin counts, label noise, and reward guidance strength. These directly investigate conflict resolution, controllability, and robustness. v1 Figure 2's benchmark learning curves are removed, while its training-regime comparison is expanded in v2 Table 3.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added human-ranking and agreement metrics remain point estimates rather than introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: All 210 numerical entries in main Tables 1–2 are unchanged, as are the retained implicit-reward accuracy and training-correlation tables. v2 adds substantial results, including conflict-only average win rates of 77.0 for MCDPO versus 59.0 for DPO, temporal-guidance CLIP performance of 59.6, and human mean rank 2.14 for MCDPO. Some retained cells also change, such as the conditional aesthetic specialist's aesthetic score from 88.0 to 88.1. Added configurations are not same-setting version-to-version gains.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.2 adds an effective-reward definition and a claimed optimality derivation connecting the conditional implicit reward to the disentangled BT target, under capacity and conditioning assumptions. Section 3.3 consequently replaces a conceptual gradient analogy with an asserted equivalence. v2 also removes v1 Eq. 10's comparison inequality and corrects the denoising residual norms in Eq. 6 to squared norms.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain conditional multi-reward DPO, sample efficiency, and inference-time preference control without additional training. The introduction adds the specific claim that conflict-only MCDPO surpasses randomly trained standard DPO. The abstract's 18% and 3% training-data figures foreground efficiency evidence already reported in v1.

C2.justification: The explanation of superiority to specialists shifts from resolving their hidden reward conflicts to a conjecture about reducing reward overfitting through cross-dimensional references. v2 adds an early-semantics/late-aesthetics rationale for temporal guidance and qualifies exact reward decomposition by conditioning capacity. The proxy-judge and preprocessing limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents normalized reward discretization into 100 bins, AdamW versus Adafactor, 50-step DDIM sampling, and selection of each method's best CFG scale. Appendix C revises pretraining hyperparameters. The main GPU-hour totals are equivalent to v1, but the appendix introduces an inconsistency by describing 16 SD1.5 GPU hours as 2 GPUs multiplied by 6 hours.

R1.justification: v2 adds the AdamW and Adafactor references and removes Provably Robust DPO, Robust Preference Optimization via Dynamic Target Margins, and beta-DPO. Positioning relative to parameter merging, sequential alignment, reward-conditioned SFT, and conflict-free filtering remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The method justification and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten and reorganized. Standard DPO specialists move from Appendix B into the main analysis, component ablations move to the end of Section 4.3, and conclusion and limitations are consolidated. The appendices are reorganized around interpolation, implementation, human evaluation, robustness, and qualitative examples.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main paper from two columns to a single-column layout, with reflowed equations, narrower or wrapped tables, and resized figures. It removes v1 Figure 2, adds conflict trajectories and agreement heatmaps, introduces Tables 3 and 10–13, and expands retained tables. The qualitative image grids contain the same images, relocated and resized.

improvement.justification: The added conflict-only controls, matched comparisons, and sensitivity analyses better test the central conflict-resolution claim, while implementation disclosures improve reproducibility. These support a net improvement, tempered by weaknesses in the additions: the human study omits evaluator details and its Table 11 Top-1 rates total 78.9% without explanation, while Appendix C introduces inconsistent GPU-time arithmetic. The revision strengthens validation but leaves meaningful reporting concerns.
